following document is intended as a guide for testers working on validation testing for new Blazor features.\n\n## What we are testing\n\nTesting scenarios are published as issues in the `dotnet/aspnetcore` repository labeled with the [`validation-scenario` label](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20state%3Aopen%20label%3Avalidation-scenario).\n\nFor each scenario, you are asked to build a small, real application, using the same packages, templates, and tooling a customer would use. The goal is comprehensive testing that covers multiple angles:\n\n1. **Correctness.** Does the feature behave as described, in every configuration the scenario lists, on the build that will ship?\n2. **Developer experience.** Was the feature discoverable and easy to use? Were the APIs, defaults, and error messages clear?\n3. **Documentation.** Could you accomplish the task using the published documentation alone, and was it accurate and complete?\n\nWhile testing a feature, **do not study its implementation** in the repository. Use links provided in the scenario description, or search for public user-facing information such as release notes or MSDN pages. Read the XML documentation for the tested APIs surfaced by the IDE (mouse over, F12).\n\n## Before you start\n\n### Install and verify the build\n\nScenarios are validated against the current .NET 11 preview or release candidate. Which of the two routes below you need depends on whether the build you want has shipped yet. Prefer a released build whenever the scenario's minimum build has shipped, and use a daily build only when it has not.\n\n**A released preview.** Download the SDK from the [.NET 11 downloads page](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/11.0). Every release is listed in the [.NET 11 release notes](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/README.md), which is the quickest way to confirm the exact version string.\n\n**A build that has not shipped yet.** Take the daily build for the release branch from the [.NET SDK builds table](https://github.com/dotnet/dotnet/blob/main/docs/builds-table.md), which carries one column per active branch. For example, for the .NET 11 Preview 7 branch on Windows x64 that is [dotnet-sdk-win-x64.exe](https://aka.ms/dotnet/11.0.1xx-preview7/daily/dotnet-sdk-win-x64.exe), and the matching [productCommit-win-x64.txt](https://aka.ms/dotnet/11.0.1xx-preview7/daily/productCommit-win-x64.txt) records the exact commits it was built from. Daily builds change without notice, so record that commit next to the version number and include it in your report.\n\nVerify what versions you actually have:\n\n```bash\ndotnet --info\ndotnet --list-sdks\ndotnet --list-runtimes\n```\n\nPin the SDK so that another installation cannot silently take over:\n\n```bash\ndotnet new globaljson --sdk-version \u003cversion\u003e --roll-forward latestPatch\n```\n\nCommit that `global.json` with your sample app. It is what makes your result reproducible later.\n\n### Visual Studio, Visual Studio Code, and workloads\n\nPreview SDKs need preview IDE tooling:\n\n- **Visual Studio 2026:** Install the [Preview channel](https://visualstudio.microsoft.com/vs/preview/). Then enable **Tools \u003e Options \u003e Environment \u003e Preview Features \u003e Use previews of the .NET SDK** and restart, otherwise the IDE will quietly fall back to an older SDK.\n- **Visual Studio Code:** Install the C# Dev Kit, and switch it to the **pre-release version**.\n\nSome scenarios need workloads on top of the SDK:\n\n* `dotnet workload install wasm-tools`, for publishing a WebAssembly app trimmed or ahead-of-time compiled.\n* `dotnet workload install maui`, for the Hybrid scenarios.\n\n### Package feeds\n\nFor a released preview, nuget.org is enough. Preview packages are published there, so no `NuGet.config` is needed.\n\nFor a daily build, add a `NuGet.config` next to your app:\n\n```xml\n\u003c?xml version=\"1.0\" encoding=\"utf-8\"?\u003e\n\u003cconfiguration\u003e\n    \u003cpackageSources\u003e\n        \u003cclear /\u003e\n        \u003cadd key=[REDACTED] value=\"https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/dnceng/public/_packaging/dotnet11/nuget/v3/index.json\" /\u003e\n        \u003cadd key=[REDACTED] value=\"https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json\" /\u003e\n    \u003c/packageSources\u003e\n\u003c/configuration\u003e\n```\n\nKeep that file with the app rather than editing the machine-wide configuration. Commit it with the sample app alongside `global.json`.\n\n### Set up somewhere to put evidence\n\nCreate a folder for the scenario before you start and drop artifacts into it as you go (screenshots, logs, recordings, etc.).\n\n## Building the app\n\nWork the way a developer would who is meeting this feature for the first time and has a problem to solve.\n\n* Start from the stated template and keep the app small enough that the feature is the thing you are dealing with.\n* Reach the feature only through public entry points: packages, templates, public APIs, tooling. Do not reverse-engineer the implementation from the dotnet repository.\n* Write friction down while it is happening.\n\n### Using AI assistance\n\nGenerally speaking, there are three levels of using AI during validation testing:\n\n1. You write the sample code manually and test the app manually. AI is either not involved, or only provides local help such as code completions.\n2. You task an AI agent to write the sample code, then you test the app manually.\n3. An AI agent both writes the sample code and tests the app (using browser automation and related tools).\n\nThe valuable contribution comes from working at the first and/or second level. The third level can be covered by automated workflows.\n\nIdeally, you would work with the feature both manually and with the help of an AI assistant, and report the experience in both cases. While building with AI, follow these rules:\n\n* **Do not let an AI assistant read the framework source or the implementation pull requests.** Otherwise the assistant can work around issues and limitations of the implementation automatically, decreasing the value of the test.\n* **Verify any finding before reporting it.** When an assistant flags an issue, reason about its relevancy and verify it manually.\n\nExample of an opening prompt:\n\n```text\nYou are helping me build a small sample app to validate a .NET 11 Blazor feature before it ships. Work only from public documentation, the package APIs, and compiler/test output. Do not read the ASP.NET Core source, the implementation pull requests, or issue threads, and do not search for them.\n\nIf something appears broken, undocumented, or harder than it should be, stop and tell me instead of working around it.\n```\n\n### Configurations\n\nEach scenario lists the configurations it applies to. A ticked box means the configuration is relevant to that scenario, not that it has already been tested.\n\nThe commands below assume you have pinned the SDK with `global.json` first, so the app is created by the build under test.\n\n#### Blazor Web App\n\nYou can use **one app for all four render modes**.\n\n```bash\ndotnet new blazor -n MyScenarioApp -int Auto\n```\n\nThis registers both `AddInteractiveServerComponents()` and `AddInteractiveWebAssemblyComponents()`, maps both render modes, and creates two projects: `MyScenarioApp` and `MyScenarioApp.Client`.\n\nAdd `-ai` (`--all-interactive`) to apply the render mode globally at the root instead of per page. Without it, pages are statically rendered by default and you opt in per component via the `@rendermode` directive:\n\n| Configuration | How to get it |\n|---|---|\n| Static SSR | No `@rendermode` on the component |\n| Interactive Server | `@rendermode InteractiveServer` |\n| Interactive WebAssembly | `@rendermode InteractiveWebAssembly`, component must live in the `.Client` project |\n| Interactive Auto | `@rendermode InteractiveAuto`, component must live in the `.Client` project |\n\nTo set a mode globally instead, put it on `\u003cRoutes /\u003e` and `\u003cHeadOutlet /\u003e` in `Components/App.razor`.\n\n**In Visual Studio:** File \u003e New \u003e Project \u003e **Blazor Web App**. On the **Additional information** page set:\n\n* **Interactive render mode** — `Auto (Server and WebAssembly)`. `Server` and `WebAssembly` limit you to that one mode, `None` gives static SSR only and no `.Client` project.\n* **Interactivity location** — `Per page/component` to opt in per component, or `Global` for the whole app. This is disabled when the render mode is `None` or when authentication is enabled.\n* **Include sample pages** — keep these on unless the scenario says otherwise, they give you something to click through.\n\n#### Standalone WebAssembly\n\nA separate app. It has no render modes, everything runs in the browser, and it cannot do static SSR.\n\n```bash\ndotnet new blazorwasm -n MyScenarioWasm\n```\n\nAdd `-p` (`--pwa`) if the scenario involves installation or offline behavior.\n\n**In Visual Studio:** File \u003e New \u003e Project \u003e **Blazor WebAssembly Standalone App**. The **Additional information** page has no interactivity options, since there are none to choose. Tick **Progressive Web Application** if the scenario needs it.\n\n#### Hybrid (MAUI)\n\nA separate app. It always renders interactively in a WebView, and `@rendermode` annotations have no effect there.\n\n```bash\ndotnet workload install maui\ndotnet new maui-blazor -n MyScenarioHybrid\n```\n\nUse `maui-blazor-web` instead when the scenario asks you to share components between a Hybrid app and a Blazor Web App. It creates both plus a shared library:\n\n```bash\ndotnet new maui-blazor-web -n MyScenarioShared -int Auto\n```\n\n**In Visual Studio:** you need the **.NET MAUI** workload installed through the Visual Studio Installer. Then File \u003e New \u003e Project \u003e **.NET MAUI Blazor Hybrid App**, or **.NET MAUI Blazor Hybrid and Web App** for the shared-UI variant, which asks for the web app's interactive render mode.\n\nBuilding for a device or emulator needs the platform SDKs, so allow extra time the first time you run this.\n\n#### Interactive Auto is two runs\n\nInteractive Auto runs on Server for a first visit and on WebAssembly once resources are cached, so it is **two different runs of the same page**. Test a fresh visit with browser storage cleared, then reload once the app is cached, and report both. Note that the modes are switched after the reload, not automatically during one session (a common misconception).\n\n### Beyond the first run\n\nScenarios build and run in **Debug** unless the scenario ticks **Published output**, in which case also run the published Release build and report the two separately when they differ.\n\nThe items below are independent options, not a sequence. Each scenario's **Also exercise** checklist says which of them apply to it, so work from that rather than through this list.\n\n* **Publish and run the published output.** Several .NET 11 issues appeared only in published applications.\n\n  ```bash\n  dotnet publish -c Release\n  ```\n\n* **Upgrade an existing app.** Where the scenario says so, start from an application built on the previous version and move it forward, rather than starting from a new template. Upgrades surface a different class of problem than new projects: new warnings on existing code, behavior that changes silently, and APIs that are gone.\n* **Trimming and ahead-of-time compilation.** WebAssembly applications are published trimmed, and anything relying on reflection, resources, or serialization can behave differently there than during development.\n* **A proxy or a sub-path in front.** Anything touching URLs, assets, or redirects behaves differently once the app is not at the root of a host. Where the scenario mentions more than one server instance, run two and route between them without sticky sessions.\n* **Hot Reload.** Run the app from source with Hot Reload enabled in an IDE, or with `dotnet watch` from the console. Change something and save, then see if this triggers hot reload and if the changes are properly reflected in the running app. This applies to a Debug run from source, not to published output.\n* **An IDE as well as the command line.** Do the same steps in Visual Studio or VS Code and at the command line, and report where they disagree: different diagnostics, different build output, or a feature that only surfaces in one of them.\n* **Container.** Run the app in a container, either through the template's container support or the IDE's container tooling.\n\nIf you skip one that the scenario asked for, say so in the report rather than leaving it ambiguous.\n\n## What to watch for\n\nCheck all of these as you work, and capture anything unexpected, unhelpful, or noisy, including things that turn out to be harmless:\n\n* Build errors and warnings, including analyzer diagnostics, their identifiers, and their suggested code fixes.\n* Runtime exceptions, and whether the message says what to do rather than only what failed.\n* .NET console output, including logs that are too noisy as well as ones that are missing.\n* Browser console output and errors.\n* Browser network activity, when the scenario involves navigation, assets, downloads, or reconnection.\n* The visual result and layout, including what happens in the moments while the page is still loading.\n* Accessibility where the feature renders UI: keyboard reachability, focus behavior, and whether labels, errors, and status changes are announced.\n* Time and resource use over a longer session, where the scenario involves repeated actions.\n\nTake a screenshot of anything that looks wrong.\n\n## Evidence\n\nMatch the evidence to the kind of claim. Capture it for passes too, not only failures: a pass with nothing behind it cannot be told apart later from a scenario nobody ran.\n\n| What you are claiming | What to capture |\n|---|---|\n| An HTTP or wire behavior | The request and the full response, headers included. `curl -i` output pasted as text. |\n| Rendered output | A screenshot, plus the relevant markup copied from developer tools. |\n| A build or analyzer behavior | The full build output showing the diagnostic identifier and the line. |\n| A runtime failure | The complete exception and stack trace, the .NET console output, and the browser console output. |\n| Something about timing, flicker, or a transition | A short screen recording. |\n| Memory or resource growth | Before and after measurements, and how long the session ran. |\n| Any finding at all | The exact steps to reproduce, starting from the `dotnet new` command. |\n\n## Publishing your sample app\n\nPublish the app as an ordinary GitHub repository under your own account or your organization, and put the link in your report. You can use folders inside a shared repository.\n\n* Link the exact place the app lives, so a reviewer lands on the code rather than on a repository root they have to search.\n* Include a short README with the scenario title, the build you tested, and how to run each configuration you covered.\n* Commit `global.json`, and the `NuGet.config` if you used a daily build, so the app restores against the same bits later.\n* Leave the app in the state that shows the finding. If you carried on working afterwards, say so, or link the commit that shows it.\n\n## Reporting\n\nReport using comments on the scenario issue. Use one comment per configuration where results differ between them.\n\n```markdown\n### Test report\n\n* **Build tested:** (full SDK version from `dotnet --info`)\n* **Configurations tested:**\n* **Also exercised:** (which **Also exercise** boxes you covered, or \"none\")\n* **OS, browser, IDE:**\n* **Sample app:** (link to the repository or the folder inside it)\n* **Outcome:** works / works with issues / blocked\n\n#### Checks\n\n| Check | Result | Evidence |\n|---|---|---|\n| (each \"Must hold\" item from the scenario) | pass / fail / not run | (link or attachment) |\n\n#### Problems\n\n1. **(Classification)** Short summary.\n   - What happened, what you expected instead, and the steps to reproduce.\n   - Evidence: (attachment or link)\n   - See section *Classifying problems* below.\n\n#### Not covered\n\n(Checks or steps you did not get to, and why.)\n```\n\n### Classifying problems\n\nLabel each finding with one of these so results can be grouped later:\n\n* **Product bug.** The framework behaves incorrectly, crashes, or produces the wrong output.\n* **Diagnostic quality.** An error, warning, or log was missing, wrong, misleading, or unhelpful.\n* **DX friction.** It works, but it was confusing, awkward, verbose, or hard to discover.\n* **Documentation gap.** Documentation was missing, incorrect, incomplete, or hard to find.\n* **Accessibility.** Something is unreachable, unannounced, or unusable without a mouse.\n* **Scenario problem.** The scenario itself is wrong, unclear, or impossible as written.\n\n## When a scenario is done\n\nA scenario counts as **validated** when all of the following hold:\n\n* Every **Must hold** check passed.\n* Every ticked configuration was covered, along with anything ticked under **Also exercise**.\n* The run was on a build at or after the scenario's **Minimum build**.\n* Each result has evidence attached that someone else can open.\n\n**Results do not carry forward between builds.** A pass on an early preview says nothing about the release candidate, because the code changed underneath it. Expect scenarios to be re-run as later builds appear, and always state which build a result belongs to.\n\nWhere a scenario was only partly covered, say so under **Not covered** and leave it open. A partial pass reported as a pass is worse than no result, because nobody goes back to it.\n\nEach scenario has its **contact person** named at the top of the description. When you have finished working on the scenario and have posted the report as a comment, **assign the scenario issue to the contact**. The scenario contact is responsible for closing the issue. contact:** @javiercn\n\n## Scenario\n\nOther ASP.NET Core templates have long offered **Enable container support** in the project creation dialog. The Blazor Web App template did not, so teams deploying to containers had to add a Dockerfile by hand. In .NET 11 the IDE can generate Docker support for the Blazor Web App template too. What needs validating is that the Dockerfile the IDE produces builds and runs the app correctly.\n\nThat matters most for the **two-project shapes**. Interactive WebAssembly and Interactive Auto generate a server project plus a `.Client` project, and a Dockerfile has to get the build context and project references right for both. Blazor Web App is the first template offering this option that has that shape.\n\n## Minimum build\n\n.NET 11 Preview 7 or later.\n\n## Configurations to cover\n\n* Blazor Web App\n  * [x] Static SSR\n  * [x] Interactive Server\n  * [x] Interactive WebAssembly\n  * [x] Interactive Auto\n* [ ] Standalone WebAssembly\n* [ ] Hybrid (MAUI)\n\nAll four are ticked because the project layout differs between them, and the layout is what the Dockerfile has to cope with. The first two produce one project, the last two produce two.\n\n## Also exercise\n\n* [x] Published output\n* [ ] An existing .NET 10 app upgraded to .NET 11\n* [ ] Trimming or ahead-of-time compilation\n* [ ] More than one server instance, or a proxy in front\n* [ ] Hot Reload\n* [ ] An IDE as well as the command line\n* [x] Container\n\n## Setup\n\nVisual Studio with the container tooling installed, and a working container runtime.\n\nThis option exists only in the IDE project creation dialog. `dotnet new blazor` has no equivalent switch, so this scenario cannot be driven from the command line. If you cannot find the option, that is itself the finding.\n\n## What to build\n\nCreate a Blazor Web App four times from the project creation dialog, once per interactivity choice, ticking **Enable container support** each time. Keep the sample content so there is something to click through.\n\nTo each app, add one page that loads an image and a stylesheet from the app's own `wwwroot`, so a missing static asset in the image is visible rather than silent.\n\n## Things to try\n\n* Finding the container option in the creation dialog for the Blazor Web App template.\n* Building and running each of the four apps in a container immediately after creation, changing nothing.\n* Clicking through the sample pages in the container, including the interactive ones, and loading your static-asset page.\n* Reading the generated Dockerfile for the two-project shapes, checking how the `.Client` project is restored and copied.\n* Running the same project outside a container.\n* Publishing an image and running it outside the IDE.\n* Creating the app with the option switched off, then adding container support from the project context menu afterwards, and comparing the result.\n\n## Expected behavior\n\nThe option is offered, and the app it produces runs in a container without hand-editing.\n\n### Must hold\n\n* The creation dialog offers **Enable container support** for the Blazor Web App template, in the same place as for other ASP.NET Core templates.\n* All four apps build a container image and run in it with no manual edits to the Dockerfile or the project files.\n* In the container, every sample page works, interactivity starts, and the image and stylesheet on your own page load with no 404 in the browser network log.\n* The two-project shapes behave the same as the single-project ones, with the `.Client` project's assets present in the image.\n* The same projects still build and run outside a container.\n* A published image runs on its own outside the IDE.\n\n## Evidence to Summary\r\n\r\n`src/Components/Web.JS/src/Services/NavigationEnhancement.ts`'s `onDocumentSubmit` handler currently detects two cases where a form cannot be enhanced, and logs a runtime `console.warn` for each:\r\n\r\n```ts\r\nconst method = event.submitter?.getAttribute('formmethod') || formElem.method;\r\nif (method === 'dialog') {\r\n  console.warn('A form cannot be enhanced when its method is \"dialog\".');\r\n  return;\r\n}\r\n\r\nconst target = event.submitter?.getAttribute('formtarget') || formElem.target;\r\nif (target !== '' \u0026\u0026 target !== '_self') {\r\n  console.warn('A form cannot be enhanced when its target is different from the default value \"_self\".');\r\n  return;\r\n}\r\n```\r\n\r\nBoth are genuine functional issues (the form silently falls back to a full page load instead of being enhanced), not style preferences, so a warning is justified. However, both conditions are driven by static attributes on the `\u003cform\u003e` / submit button (`method` / `formmethod`, `target` / `formtarget`) that are almost always known at compile time from the `.razor` markup.\r\n\r\n## Ask\r\n\r\nInvestigate whether a build-time Roslyn analyzer (in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Analyzers`) can detect these same two cases directly from `.razor` markup: a `\u003cform\u003e` (or `\u003cEditForm\u003e`) with a literal `method=\"dialog\"`, or a literal `target` / `formtarget` value other than `\"\"` / `\"_self\"`, combined with enhanced navigation being enabled (the default, i.e. not opted out via `data-enhance-nav=\"false\"` or similar).\r\n\r\nIf feasible, this would let developers catch the misconfiguration in the editor / at compile time instead of only discovering it at runtime via the console warning, the same motivation discussed for the Virtualize spacer-element case.\r\n\r\n## Constraint\r\n\r\nThe analyzer can only fire when the value is a static literal. Dynamic or data-bound `method` / `target` / `formmethod` / `formtarget` values (e.g. `method=\"@someExpression\"`) cannot be analyzed statically, so the runtime `console.warn` must remain as the fallback for those Please describe the problem.\n\n## Proposal: Enhancing Component Visibility in Blazor\n\n### Description\nI am developing a Blazor component library that is consumed by various teams within our organization. During this process, we have identified the need to create internal components that should not be exposed outside of the library.\n\nHowever, we have encountered a limitation where Razor components in Blazor are required to have public visibility by default. This restriction prevents us from properly encapsulating components that we don't want to make accessible outside the library, which reduces our control over the exposure of our code.\n\n### Problem\n- Razor components in Blazor are **public by default** due to inheriting from `ComponentBase`.\n- There is **no option** to define internal or restricted components that are only intended to be used within the assembly or library.\n- This limitation **exposes unnecessary components** that are not intended to be accessed externally, impacting the modularity and encapsulation of the library.\n\n\n\n### Impact\nThis change would provide more flexibility in how components are designed and structured in Blazor projects. It would help create cleaner, more modular libraries without affecting existing applications, as `public` components would still be fully supported.\n\n\nI believe it would significantly enhance the development experience for Blazor component libraries.\n\n\n### Describe the solution you'd like\n\n### Proposal\n- Introduce the ability for Razor components to have more restrictive visibility levels, such as `internal` or `protected`.\n- This would allow developers to encapsulate components that should remain internal to the library or assembly, improving **modularity** and **code currently only exposes an `AuthenticationState` context to the `NotAuthorized` render fragment. It does not provide access to the full `AuthorizationResult`, including `AuthorizationFailureReason` messages set by custom authorization handlers.\n\n### Problem\n\nWhen implementing custom authorization handlers that use `context.Fail(new AuthorizationFailureReason(...))` to provide detailed failure messages, there is no supported way to surface these messages in the `NotAuthorized` render fragment.\n\nThe current implementation in `AuthorizeViewCore.IsAuthorizedAsync()` discards the full authorization result:\n\n```csharp\nvar result = await AuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, Resource, policy!);\nreturn result.Succeeded; // Only boolean is returned, AuthorizationResult is lost\n```\n\n### Proposed Solution\n\nIntroduce a new `Forbidden` render fragment that handles the \"authenticated but not authorized\" (403) case separately from `NotAuthorized`. This new fragment would have a context type that includes `AuthorizationResult` and failure reasons, enabling developers to display detailed error messages. streaming rendering or not), there isn't a clear visual feedback mechanism to inform end-users that something is happening in the background.\n\n**Current Issues:**\n- Users clicking navigation links don't see any indication that the page is loading\n- Form submissions (particularly authentication forms, search forms, etc.) appear unresponsive until the server responds\n- This creates a poor user experience, as users might think the application is frozen or broken, causing them to click twice, three times, or even more\n- **Attempting to handle this manually (e.g., disabling form controls on submit) breaks Blazor's form submission logic**\n- There's no way to prevent duplicate submissions or input changes during form processing without breaking functionality\n\nThis is particularly problematic for:\n- Search or filter forms where users need feedback that their action was received\n- Any navigation or form interaction where latency might cause delays\n- Pages using `[ExcludeFromInteractiveRouting]` which have no built-in feedback mechanism\n\n### Describe the solution you'd like\n\nImplement a built-in navigation and form-submission feedback mechanism for Blazor Static SSR, similar in spirit to [htmx’s indicator system](https://htmx.org/docs/#indicators).\n\n**Goal:** provide consistent, automatic visual and UX feedback during:\n- Page navigations (enhanced navigation and pages using `[ExcludeFromInteractiveRouting]`, with or without streaming rendering)\n- Form submissions (including common scenarios like auth, search, and filtering)\n\n**Proposed behavior:**\n1. **Navigation indicators**\n   - Allow developers to designate indicator elements (e.g., `\u003cdiv class=\"navigation-indicator\"\u003eLoading...\u003c/div\u003e`).\n   - When navigation starts, Blazor automatically toggles a predictable CSS state (for example adding a `.navigating` / `.show` class, or setting an attribute like `data-blazor-state=\"navigating\"`), and removes it when navigation completes.\n\n2. **Form submission indicators**\n   - Allow developers to designate indicator elements for form submits (e.g., `\u003cdiv class=\"form-indicator\"\u003eSubmitting...\u003c/div\u003e`).\n   - When a form submit begins, Blazor automatically toggles a predictable CSS state (e.g., `.submitting` / `.show`, or `data-blazor-state=\"submitting\"`) and clears it when the submit completes (success or failure).\n\n3. **Automatic control disabling (opt-in)**\n   - Support an opt-in attribute such as `data-disable-on-submit` that can be applied to a `fieldset` or individual inputs/buttons.\n   - While a submission is in progress, Blazor temporarily disables the annotated controls to prevent duplicate submissions and input changes, then restores the prior enabled/disabled state afterward.\n   - This should work with both enhanced navigation form posts and forms on pages using ProjectId { get; set; }\n    public int? DepartmentId { get; set; }\n}\n```\nThe problem is that SecurityContext in dynamicly set from url, but attribute can contains only static info. So it is not an option. \n2. **Layout Approach**\n   - Attempted to use multiple layouts to handle authorization states, but Blazor only supports a single layout per page.\n\n3. **Inheritance Approach**\n   - Implemented a base component (`SecurityComponentBaseCore` + `SecurityComponentBase`) that handles loading, access checks, and error messages.\n\n### Example: `SecurityComponentBaseCore.razor`\n```razor\n@if (Loading)\n{\n    \u003cFluentStack HorizontalAlignment=\"HorizontalAlignment.Center\" VerticalAlignment=\"VerticalAlignment.Center\" Style=\"height: 100%\"\u003e\n        \u003cFluentProgressRing style=\"width: 62px; height: 62px;\" /\u003e\n    \u003c/FluentStack\u003e\n}\nelse if (HasAccess)\n{\n    @Body\n}\nelse\n{\n    \u003cFluentMessageBar Intent=\"MessageIntent.Warning\"\u003e@ErrorMessage\u003c/FluentMessageBar\u003e\n}\n\n@code {\n    public virtual bool Loading { get; set; } = true;\n    public virtual bool HasAccess { get; set; } = false;\n    public virtual string ErrorMessage { get; set; } = string.Empty;\n    private protected virtual RenderFragment Body =\u003e builder =\u003e { };\n}\n```\n\n### Example: `SecurityComponentBase.cs`\n```csharp\npublic abstract class SecurityComponentBase : SecurityComponentBaseCore\n{\n    [Inject] protected ISecurityManager SecurityManager { get; set; } = default!;\n    [Inject] protected ILogger\u003cSecurityComponentBase\u003e Logger { get; set; } = default!;\n\n    protected virtual SecurityContext Context { get; } = new SecurityContext();\n    protected virtual List\u003cstring\u003e RequiredPermissions { get; } = [];\n\n    private protected sealed override RenderFragment Body =\u003e BuildRenderTree;\n    protected new virtual void BuildRenderTree(RenderTreeBuilder builder) { }\n\n    protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync()\n    {\n        try\n        {\n            Loading = true;\n            var res = await SecurityManager.HasAccess(Context, RequiredPermissions);\n\n            HasAccess = res.IsSuccess;\n            Loading = false;\n            if (!HasAccess)\n            {\n                ErrorMessage = res.ErrorMessage ?? \"Access denied\";\n            }\n        }\n        catch (Exception ex)\n        {\n            Logger.LogError(ex, \"Error checking permissions\");\n            HasAccess = false;\n            ErrorMessage = \"Error checking permissions\";\n        }\n        finally\n        {\n            Loading = false;\n        }\n    }\n}\n```\n### Example: `MyComponent.razor`\n```razor\n@inherits SecurityComponentBase\n\n\u003cdiv\u003e\n    content\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\n@code {\n    protected override List\u003cstring\u003e RequiredPermissions { get; Without this re‑render, the loader remains visible longer than intended.\n\n---\n\n\n# Question\n\nIs there a proper Blazor solution that allows building an `Authorize`-like mechanism with:\n\n- A loader displayed during the permission check  \n- A custom denied fragment that shows missing rights  \n- The ability to pass both a list of required permissions and a context model (`SecurityContext`)  \n\nIs there a recommended pattern or framework support for this scenario?  \nAlternatively, could the existing `Authorize` attribute be extended or modified to handle these requirements?\n\nAttempting to implement something that was not originally intended feels fragile, especially since Blazor evolves quickly and such a workaround may stop functioning in future versions (I have already experienced this).  \n\nTherefore, the core question is: **Is there a proper, supported way to create an equivalent of `Authorize` or a reworked version that will reliably function in Blazor?**\n\nIt is possible that I have not fully understood all aspects of Blazor’s authorization system and may be missing something important. Background\r\n\r\nWe've seen a few issue reports (e.g., #47824, #44974) where customers attempt to use the `required` modifier on Blazor component parameter properties to ensure that the parameter will definitely have a value assigned to it.\r\n\r\n## Why this is a problem\r\n\r\nThis is not a supported pattern (and it likely never will be) because Blazor component parameters do not get assigned upon component instantiation. Instead, a `ParameterView` object gets passed to the component's `SetParametersAsync` method, which updates parameter property values accordingly. The `required` modifier has no bearing on whether the parameter will have an entry in the `ParameterView`. Furthermore, even for parameters that _do_ have `ParameterView` entries, their properties won't get values assigned until long after what the `required` modifier is supposed to guarantee.\r\n\r\nCurrently, using the `required` modifier in a Blazor component doesn't break anything, because any component extending `ComponentBase` (or otherwise manually invoking `ParameterView.SetParameterProperties()`) gets its properties set via refelction. But the `required` modifier can mislead component authors into thinking that it will make the property \"required\", especially considering it makes nullability warnings go away.\r\n\r\nLikewise, `init` has no effect in any component whose parameters are set using `ParameterView.SetParameterProperties()`, because reflection bypasses the \"init-only\" restriction.\r\n\r\nIf we implement #29550, then using `required` or `init` could cause compilation errors, since we won't be using reflection to bypass the restrictions that `required` or `init` impose. Therefore, for future-proofing reasons, it's in our best interest to ensure that customers avoid using these keywords on Blazor component properties.\r\n\r\n## Proposed solution\r\n\r\nFor all these reasons, we should consider implementing an analyzer that emits a warning whenever component properties use `required` or `init`. The analyzer message can suggest using the `[EditorRequired]` attribute Summary\r\n\r\nBlazor server apps authenticate the user at the beginning of the circuit lifetime and offer a mechanism for updating the principal when used in conjunction with identity. The way Blazor Server handles authentication is confusing for some users since they are used to the authentication to be re-validated on every request/response, as opposed to Blazor, for which the authentication by default lasts the entire lifetime of the circuit.\r\n\r\n## Motivation and goals\r\n\r\n*  This aspect of Blazor server authentication is a common point of confusion we receive frequent feedback about.\r\n* There are plenty of issues on our GH repo about this problem.\r\n\r\n## In scope\r\n\r\nProvide a mechanism that lets the server initiate a request for re-validating the user credentials and updating the Principal accordingly.\r\n\r\nThe general idea is to provide an endpoint that receives a protected payload TBD, authenticates the user and returns a protected payload with the updated authentication context that the server can validate and use to update the Principal before the next authorization check.\r\n\r\n## Out of scope\r\n\r\nRe-validating authentication is limited to authenticating the user against the schemes defined by a policy, there is no way to customize this process besides that.\r\n\r\n## Risks / unknowns\r\n\r\nThis is a security related feature, so it needs to be thread model analysis.\r\n\r\n## Examples\r\n\r\n`@attribute [RevalidateAuthentication]`\r\n\r\nThe authorizerouteview would check this attribute on the handler and act accordingly.\r\n\r\nThere would also be an imperative API that can be used from event handlers to check this.\r\n```csharp\r\nawait Summary\n\n`AuthorizeViewCore` currently calls `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(...)` to determine whether a user is authorized, but only keeps the boolean `Succeeded` value from `AuthorizationResult`. The complete authorization result, including `AuthorizationFailureReason` values, is discarded before rendering.\n\nThis prevents applications from displaying meaningful authorization failure messages in Blazor UI.\n\nThis proposal updates `AuthorizeViewCore` to preserve the full `AuthorizationResult` and expose authorization failure details through authorization-related template contexts.\n\nThe design adds:\n\n1. A new `AuthorizationStateWithResult` type that extends `AuthenticationState` and includes `AuthorizationResult`.\n2. A new `Forbidden` render fragment for authenticated users who fail authorization.\n3. Updated fallback behavior so `NotAuthorized` can receive an `AuthorizationStateWithResult` instance when authorization fails and `Forbidden` is not supplied.\n\nThis addresses both linked issues:\n\n- \u003chttps://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/43959\u003e\n- \u003chttps://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/65056\u003e\n\n---\n\n## Problem\n\nBlazor's `AuthorizeViewCore` currently evaluates authorization and renders one of the existing fragments:\n\n- `Authorizing`\n- `Authorized`\n- `ChildContent`\n- `NotAuthorized`\n\nThe authorization result is reduced to a boolean value:\n\n```csharp\nresult.Succeeded\n```\n\nAs a result, metadata from `AuthorizationResult` is lost.\n\nThis is a problem because custom authorization handlers can produce useful failure reasons:\n\n```csharp\ncontext.Fail(\n    new AuthorizationFailureReason(\n        this,\n        \"Missing permission: Project.Read\"));\n```\n\nToday, `AuthorizeView` does not provide a supported way for Razor markup to display that failure reason.\n\nThis creates two related gaps.\n\n### Gap 1: Authorization Result Is Not Exposed\n\nApplications cannot access the following from `AuthorizeView` UI templates:\n\n```csharp\nAuthorizationResult\nAuthorizationFailure\nAuthorizationFailureReason\n```\n\nThis prevents applications from showing detailed authorization failure messages.\n\n### Gap 2: Authenticated Forbidden Users Are Not Separated from Anonymous Users\n\nToday, both anonymous users and authenticated unauthorized users generally flow through `NotAuthorized`.\n\nApplications often need different UI:\n\n```text\nAnonymous user:\nPlease sign in.\n\nAuthenticated but unauthorized user:\nYou are signed in, but you do not have permission.\n```\n\nA dedicated `Forbidden` state gives applications a clearer way to represent the authenticated-but-not-authorized case.\n\n---\n\n## Goals / Non-Goals\n\n### Goals\n\n1. Preserve the full `AuthorizationResult` returned by `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync`.\n2. Expose authorization failure reasons to Blazor templates.\n3. Add a dedicated `Forbidden` render fragment for authenticated-but-not-authorized users.\n4. Preserve existing `NotAuthorized` source compatibility.\n5. Allow `NotAuthorized` fallback scenarios to access authorization result information without changing the public `NotAuthorized` property type.\n6. Preserve existing behavior when applications do not use the new API.\n7. Keep the design simple for common Razor usage.\n8. Avoid changing policy evaluation, role evaluation, resource authorization, or authentication behavior.\n9. Provide a path that satisfies both scenarios: exposing the authorization result and separating forbidden UI from anonymous/not-authorized UI.\n\n### Non-Goals\n\n1. Do not change authorization policy semantics.\n2. Do not change authentication behavior.\n3. Do not remove or rename existing `AuthorizeView` parameters.\n4. Do not require applications to use `Forbidden`.\n5. Do not automatically sanitize, localize, or rewrite authorization failure messages.\n6. Do not introduce a general-purpose diagnostics API for authorization.\n7. Do not change routing authorization behavior outside the scope of `AuthorizeViewCore`.\n\n---\n\n## Detailed Design\n\n### Overview\n\nThe proposed design changes `AuthorizeViewCore` so that the component stores the full `AuthorizationResult` instead of only storing whether authorization succeeded.\n\nThe design introduces a new context type:\n\n```csharp\nAuthorizationStateWithResult\n```\n\nThis type derives from `AuthenticationState` and adds an `AuthorizationResult` property.\n\nThe same type is used by:\n\n1. `Forbidden`\n2. `NotAuthorized` fallback scenarios where authorization failed\n\nThis design fixes both issues:\n\n- `Forbidden` provides a clear, explicit 403-style rendering path for authenticated users who fail authorization.\n- `NotAuthorized` can still access authorization failure details when `Forbidden` is not supplied.\n\n---\n\n### New Context Type\n\nAdd a new public type:\n\n```csharp\nnamespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Authorization;\n\npublic sealed class AuthorizationStateWithResult : AuthenticationState\n{\n    public AuthorizationStateWithResult(\n        ClaimsPrincipal user,\n        AuthorizationResult authorizationResult)\n        : base(user)\n    {\n        AuthorizationResult = authorizationResult;\n    }\n\n    public AuthorizationResult AuthorizationResult { get; }\n}\n```\n\n### Purpose\n\n`AuthorizationStateWithResult` represents the current authentication state plus the result of authorization evaluation.\n\nIt allows existing `AuthenticationState`-based templates to continue working while providing access to authorization metadata in failed authorization scenarios.\n\n---\n\n### Authorization State Storage\n\n`AuthorizeViewCore` should preserve the full authorization result internally.\n\nConceptually, instead of storing only whether authorization succeeded, the component stores:\n\n```csharp\nprivate AuthorizationResult? currentAuthorizationResult;\n```\n\nThe `null` state represents that authorization is still in progress.\n\nWhen no authorization data applies to the component, the result is treated as successful:\n\n```csharp\ncurrentAuthorizationResult = AuthorizationResult.Success();\n```\n\nWhen authorization data is present, the component stores the full result returned by the authorization service:\n\n```csharp\ncurrentAuthorizationResult =\n    await AuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(\n        user,\n        Resource,\n        policy);\n```\n\n---\n\n### Existing Fragments\n\nThe existing fragments remain:\n\n```csharp\nRenderFragment\u003cAuthenticationState\u003e? ChildContent\nRenderFragment\u003cAuthenticationState\u003e? Authorized\nRenderFragment\u003cAuthenticationState\u003e? NotAuthorized\nRenderFragment? Authorizing\n```\n\n### New Fragment\n\nAdd:\n\n```csharp\nRenderFragment\u003cAuthorizationStateWithResult\u003e? Forbidden\n```\n\n---\n\n### Rendering Behavior\n\nThe conceptual rendering behavior is:\n\n```csharp\nif (authorizationResult is null)\n{\n    render Authorizing;\n}\nelse if (authorizationResult.Succeeded)\n{\n    render Authorized or ChildContent with AuthenticationState;\n}\nelse\n{\n    var stateWithResult = new AuthorizationStateWithResult(\n        currentAuthenticationState.User,\n        authorizationResult);\n\n    if (currentAuthenticationState.User.Identity?.IsAuthenticated == true \u0026\u0026\n        Forbidden is not null)\n    {\n        render Forbidden with stateWithResult;\n    }\n    else\n    {\n        render NotAuthorized with stateWithResult;\n    }\n}\n```\n\nThis means:\n\n- `Forbidden` is preferred for authenticated failed authorization.\n- `NotAuthorized` remains the fallback path.\n- Both failed authorization paths can access the full `AuthorizationResult`.\n\n---\n\n### Rendering Matrix\n\n| Scenario | Rendered Fragment | Context Type |\n|---|---|---|\n| Authorization is in progress | `Authorizing` | No context |\n| Authorization succeeds | `Authorized` or `ChildContent` | `AuthenticationState` |\n| User is anonymous and authorization fails | `NotAuthorized` | `AuthorizationStateWithResult` |\n| User is authenticated and authorization fails, `Forbidden` is supplied | `Forbidden` | `AuthorizationStateWithResult` |\n| User is authenticated and authorization fails, `Forbidden` is not supplied | `NotAuthorized` | `AuthorizationStateWithResult` |\n| No authorization data applies | `Authorized` or `ChildContent` | `AuthenticationState` |\n\n---\n\n## Public API Surface\n\n### Ref Assembly Format\n\n```csharp\nnamespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Authorization\n{\n    public sealed class AuthorizationStateWithResult : Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Authorization.AuthenticationState\n    {\n        public AuthorizationStateWithResult(\n            System.Security.Claims.ClaimsPrincipal user,\n            Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.AuthorizationResult authorizationResult);\n\n        public Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.AuthorizationResult AuthorizationResult { get; }\n    }\n\n    public abstract partial class AuthorizeViewCore : Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.ComponentBase\n    {\n        [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.ParameterAttribute]\n        public Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.RenderFragment\u003c\n            Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Authorization.AuthorizationStateWithResult\u003e? Forbidden { get; set; }\n    }\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n## `NotAuthorized` Render Fragment Behavior\n\nThe `NotAuthorized` public API remains unchanged:\n\n```csharp\n[Parameter]\npublic RenderFragment\u003cAuthenticationState\u003e? NotAuthorized { get; set; }\n```\n\nHowever, when authorization fails, the runtime context passed to `NotAuthorized` is an instance of:\n\n```csharp\nAuthorizationStateWithResult\n```\n\nBecause `AuthorizationStateWithResult` derives from `AuthenticationState`, this remains source-compatible with existing `NotAuthorized` usage.\n\nExisting code continues to work:\n\n```razor\n\u003cNotAuthorized Context=\"state\"\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ePlease sign in.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/NotAuthorized\u003e\n```\n\nAdvanced code can access the authorization result when needed:\n\n```razor\n\u003cNotAuthorized Context=\"state\"\u003e\n    @{\n        var authorizationState = state as AuthorizationStateWithResult;\n        var reason = authorizationState?.AuthorizationResult.Failure?\n            .FailureReasons.FirstOrDefault()?.Message;\n    }\n\n    \u003cp\u003e@(reason ?? \"You are not authorized.\")\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/NotAuthorized\u003e\n```\n\nThis behavior directly addresses the request to expose `AuthorizationResult` through the not-authorized rendering path while avoiding a breaking change to the existing `NotAuthorized` property type.\n\n---\n\n## `Forbidden` Render Fragment Behavior\n\n`Forbidden` is rendered when:\n\n1. Authorization has completed.\n2. Authorization failed.\n3. The current user is authenticated.\n4. The application supplied a `Forbidden` fragment.\n\nExample:\n\n```razor\n\u003cAuthorizeView Policy=\"ProjectRead\"\u003e\n    \u003cAuthorized\u003e\n        \u003cProjectDetails /\u003e\n    \u003c/Authorized\u003e\n\n    \u003cNotAuthorized\u003e\n        \u003cp\u003ePlease sign in.\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/NotAuthorized\u003e\n\n    \u003cForbidden Context=\"state\"\u003e\n        \u003cp\u003e\n            @(state.AuthorizationResult.Failure?.FailureReasons.FirstOrDefault()?.Message\n                ?? \"You do not have permission to view this project.\")\n        \u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/Forbidden\u003e\n\u003c/AuthorizeView\u003e\n```\n\n`Forbidden` provides the preferred, user-friendly API for the authenticated-but-not-authorized case.\n\n---\n\n## Customer Scenario / Use Cases\n\n### Use Case 1: Permission-Based Authorization\n\nA project management application requires `Project.Read`.\n\nWhen a signed-in user does not have the required permission, the custom authorization handler returns:\n\n```text\nMissing permission: Project.Read\n```\n\nThe application can show this message in `Forbidden`:\n\n```razor\n\u003cForbidden Context=\"state\"\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003e\n        @(state.AuthorizationResult.Failure?.FailureReasons.FirstOrDefault()?.Message\n            ?? \"You do not have permission.\")\n    \u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/Forbidden\u003e\n```\n\n---\n\n### Use Case 2: License-Based Feature Restrictions\n\nA SaaS application restricts features by license.\n\nWhen a user is authenticated but not licensed for a feature, the authorization handler can return a failure reason such as:\n\n```text\nYour license does not include Advanced Reporting.\n```\n\nThe UI can display this in `Forbidden`, allowing the application to explain why a feature is disabled or unavailable.\n\n---\n\n### Use Case 3: Existing Apps Using `NotAuthorized`\n\nAn existing app may only have:\n\n```razor\n\u003cAuthorizeView Policy=\"ProjectRead\"\u003e\n    \u003cNotAuthorized Context=\"state\"\u003e\n        \u003cp\u003eAccess denied.\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/NotAuthorized\u003e\n\u003c/AuthorizeView\u003e\n```\n\nThis app continues to work.\n\nIf the app wants access to the authorization result without adding `Forbidden`, it can cast the runtime context:\n\n```razor\n\u003cNotAuthorized Context=\"state\"\u003e\n    @{\n        var stateWithResult = state as AuthorizationStateWithResult;\n    }\n\n    @if (stateWithResult is not null)\n    {\n        \u003cp\u003e\n            @(stateWithResult.AuthorizationResult.Failure?\n                .FailureReasons.FirstOrDefault()?.Message\n                ?? \"Access denied.\")\n        \u003c/p\u003e\n    }\n    else\n    {\n        \u003cp\u003eAccess denied.\u003c/p\u003e\n    }\n\u003c/NotAuthorized\u003e\n```\n\nThis fixes the scenario where a user wants the result of `AuthorizeAsync` available from the not-authorized UI path.\n\n---\n\n### Use Case 4: Separate Anonymous and Forbidden UI\n\nApplications can separate anonymous and forbidden cases:\n\n```razor\n\u003cAuthorizeView Policy=\"CanManageBilling\"\u003e\n    \u003cAuthorized\u003e\n        \u003cBillingAdmin /\u003e\n    \u003c/Authorized\u003e\n\n    \u003cNotAuthorized\u003e\n        \u003cp\u003ePlease sign in to manage billing.\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/NotAuthorized\u003e\n\n    \u003cForbidden Context=\"state\"\u003e\n        \u003cp\u003e\n            You are signed in, but you do not have permission to manage billing.\n        \u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/Forbidden\u003e\n\u003c/AuthorizeView\u003e\n```\n\nThis provides clearer UI and better matches the 401/403 distinction.\n\n---\n\n## Proposed API Usage Examples\n\n### Example 1: Basic Forbidden UI\n\n```razor\n\u003cAuthorizeView Policy=\"CanViewReports\"\u003e\n    \u003cAuthorized\u003e\n        \u003cReportsDashboard /\u003e\n    \u003c/Authorized\u003e\n\n    \u003cNotAuthorized\u003e\n        \u003cp\u003ePlease sign in to view reports.\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/NotAuthorized\u003e\n\n    \u003cForbidden\u003e\n        \u003cp\u003eYou are signed in, but you do not have permission to view reports.\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/Forbidden\u003e\n\u003c/AuthorizeView\u003e\n```\n\n---\n\n### Example 2: Show First Authorization Failure Reason\n\n```razor\n\u003cAuthorizeView Policy=\"ProjectRead\"\u003e\n    \u003cAuthorized\u003e\n        \u003cProjectDetails /\u003e\n    \u003c/Authorized\u003e\n\n    \u003cForbidden Context=\"state\"\u003e\n        \u003cp\u003e\n            @(state.AuthorizationResult.Failure?.FailureReasons.FirstOrDefault()?.Message\n                ?? \"You do not have permission to view this project.\")\n        \u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/Forbidden\u003e\n\n    \u003cNotAuthorized\u003e\n        \u003cp\u003ePlease sign in.\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/NotAuthorized\u003e\n\u003c/AuthorizeView\u003e\n```\n\n---\n\n### Example 3: Use `NotAuthorized` Fallback with Authorization Result\n\n```razor\n\u003cAuthorizeView Policy=\"ProjectRead\"\u003e\n    \u003cAuthorized\u003e\n        \u003cProjectDetails /\u003e\n    \u003c/Authorized\u003e\n\n    \u003cNotAuthorized Context=\"state\"\u003e\n        @{\n            var authorizationState = state as AuthorizationStateWithResult;\n            var reason = authorizationState?.AuthorizationResult.Failure?\n                .FailureReasons.FirstOrDefault()?.Message;\n        }\n\n        \u003cp\u003e@(reason ?? \"You are not authorized.\")\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/NotAuthorized\u003e\n\u003c/AuthorizeView\u003e\n```\n\n---\n\n### Example 4: Display Multiple Failure Reasons\n\n```razor\n\u003cAuthorizeView Policy=\"ProjectRead\"\u003e\n    \u003cAuthorized\u003e\n        \u003cProjectDetails /\u003e\n    \u003c/Authorized\u003e\n\n    \u003cForbidden Context=\"state\"\u003e\n        @if (state.AuthorizationResult.Failure?.FailureReasons.Any() == true)\n        {\n            \u003cul\u003e\n                @foreach (var reason in state.AuthorizationResult.Failure.FailureReasons)\n                {\n                    \u003cli\u003e@reason.Message\u003c/li\u003e\n                }\n            \u003c/ul\u003e\n        }\n        else\n        {\n            \u003cp\u003eYou do not have permission to access this resource.\u003c/p\u003e\n        }\n    \u003c/Forbidden\u003e\n\n    \u003cNotAuthorized\u003e\n        \u003cp\u003ePlease sign in.\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/NotAuthorized\u003e\n\u003c/AuthorizeView\u003e\n```\n\n---\n\n### Example 5: Custom Authorization Requirement\n\n```csharp\npublic sealed record ProjectPermissionRequirement(string Permission)\n    : IAuthorizationRequirement;\n```\n\n---\n\n### Example 6: Custom Authorization Handler\n\n```csharp\npublic sealed class ProjectPermissionHandler\n    : AuthorizationHandler\u003cProjectPermissionRequirement\u003e\n{\n    protected override Task HandleRequirementAsync(\n        AuthorizationHandlerContext context,\n        ProjectPermissionRequirement requirement)\n    {\n        if (context.User.HasClaim(\"Permission\", requirement.Permission))\n        {\n            context.Succeed(requirement);\n        }\n        else\n        {\n            context.Fail(new AuthorizationFailureReason(\n                this,\n                $\"Missing permission: {requirement.Permission}\"));\n        }\n\n        return Task.CompletedTask;\n    }\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n### Example 7: Policy Registration\n\n```csharp\nbuilder.Services.AddAuthorizationCore(options =\u003e\n{\n    options.AddPolicy(\"ProjectRead\", policy =\u003e\n    {\n        policy.RequireAuthenticatedUser();\n        policy.Requirements.Add(new ProjectPermissionRequirement(\"Project.Read\"));\n    });\n});\n\nbuilder.Services.AddScoped\u003cIAuthorizationHandler, ProjectPermissionHandler\u003e();\n```\n\n---\n\n## Alternatives Considered\n\n### Alternative 1: Change `NotAuthorized` Type to Include `AuthorizationResult`\n\nExample:\n\n```csharp\npublic RenderFragment\u003cAuthorizationStateWithResult\u003e? NotAuthorized { get; set; }\n```\n\n#### Rejected\n\nThis would be a breaking change because existing users provide `RenderFragment\u003cAuthenticationState\u003e`.\n\nThe proposal avoids this by keeping the public property type unchanged:\n\n```csharp\nRenderFragment\u003cAuthenticationState\u003e?\n```\n\nand passing a derived runtime type only when authorization fails.\n\n---\n\n### Alternative 2: Only Add `Forbidden` and Do Not Update `NotAuthorized`\n\n#### Rejected\n\nThis solves the authenticated forbidden scenario but does not fully address the ask from `#43959`, where developers want authorization result information available from the unauthorized rendering path.\n\nIt also leaves fallback `NotAuthorized` without failure details when `Forbidden` is not supplied.\n\n---\n\n### Alternative 3: Add a Separate `NotAuthorizedWithResult` Fragment\n\nExample:\n\n```csharp\npublic RenderFragment\u003cAuthorizationStateWithResult\u003e? NotAuthorizedWithResult { get; set; }\n```\n\n#### Rejected\n\nThis adds another template and creates overlapping concepts:\n\n- `NotAuthorized`\n- `NotAuthorizedWithResult`\n- `Forbidden`\n\nThat would make the component harder to understand.\n\n---\n\n### Alternative 4: Add Public `AuthorizationResult` Property\n\nExample:\n\n```csharp\npublic AuthorizationResult? AuthorizationResult { get; }\n```\n\n#### Rejected\n\nThe result is needed inside render fragments. Passing the result as template context is more natural for Razor authoring.\n\n---\n\n### Alternative 5: Use Cascading Value\n\n#### Rejected\n\nA cascading value would require additional component structure and make the common scenario more complex.\n\n---\n\n## Compatibility Analysis\n\n### Source Compatibility\n\nExisting code continues to compile:\n\n```razor\n\u003cAuthorizeView Policy=\"CanViewReports\"\u003e\n    \u003cNotAuthorized\u003e\n        \u003cp\u003eAccess denied.\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/NotAuthorized\u003e\n\u003c/AuthorizeView\u003e\n```\n\nNo existing render-fragment property is removed or renamed.\n\n---\n\n### Binary Compatibility\n\nThe proposal is additive.\n\nIt adds:\n\n```csharp\nAuthorizationStateWithResult\nAuthorizeViewCore.Forbidden\n```\n\nExisting public members remain unchanged.\n\n---\n\n### Behavioral Compatibility\n\nExisting apps that do not use `Forbidden` continue to render `NotAuthorized` when authorization fails.\n\nThe main behavioral enhancement is that the runtime context passed to `NotAuthorized` in failed authorization cases may be an `AuthorizationStateWithResult`, which is still an `AuthenticationState`.\n\nExisting code that only uses:\n\n```csharp\nstate.User\n```\n\ncontinues to work.\n\n---\n\n### Razor Compatibility\n\nExisting Razor templates remain valid:\n\n```razor\n\u003cNotAuthorized Context=\"state\"\u003e\n    @state.User.Identity?.Name\n\u003c/NotAuthorized\u003e\n```\n\nAdvanced templates can opt into the richer runtime type:\n\n```razor\n\u003cNotAuthorized Context=\"state\"\u003e\n    @{\n        var stateWithResult = state as AuthorizationStateWithResult;\n    }\n\u003c/NotAuthorized\u003e\n```\n\n---\n\n## Risks and Limitations\n\n### Risk 1: Runtime Type Is Richer Than Compile-Time Type for `NotAuthorized`\n\n`NotAuthorized` remains typed as:\n\n```csharp\nAuthenticationState\n```\n\nbut in failed authorization cases receives:\n\n```csharp\nAuthorizationStateWithResult\n```\n\nThis is compatible but less discoverable than `Forbidden`.\n\n#### Mitigation\n\nDocument that `Forbidden` is the recommended template for accessing authorization failure details.\n\nDocument that `NotAuthorized` fallback can cast to `AuthorizationStateWithResult` when needed.\n\n---\n\n### Risk 2: Sensitive Failure Messages\n\nFailure reasons may include internal permission names or policy details.\n\n#### Mitigation\n\nDocumentation should warn developers to display only user-safe failure messages.\n\n---\n\n### Risk 3: Additional API Surface\n\nThe proposal adds one type and one render fragment.\n\n#### Mitigation\n\nThe new API is small and focused.\n\n---\n\n### Risk 4: Multiple Failure Reasons\n\nAuthorization can fail for multiple reasons.\n\n#### Mitigation\n\nDocumentation and tests should show how to enumerate reasons.\n\n---\n\n### Risk 5: Failed Authorization Without Failure Reasons\n\nSome failures may not include `AuthorizationFailureReason`.\n\n#### Mitigation\n\nSamples should always include fallback UI text.\n\n---\n\n## Testing Plan\n\n### Unit Tests\n\nAdd tests for:\n\n1. `Authorizing` renders while authorization is pending.\n2. `Authorized` renders when authorization succeeds.\n3. `ChildContent` renders when authorization succeeds and `Authorized` is not supplied.\n4. `Forbidden` renders for authenticated users when authorization fails.\n5. `NotAuthorized` renders for anonymous users when authorization fails.\n6. `NotAuthorized` renders as fallback when authorization fails and `Forbidden` is not supplied.\n7. `Forbidden` receives `AuthorizationStateWithResult`.\n8. `Forbidden` can access `AuthorizationResult`.\n9. `Forbidden` can access a single `AuthorizationFailureReason`.\n10. `Forbidden` can access multiple `AuthorizationFailureReason` values.\n11. `NotAuthorized` fallback receives an `AuthorizationStateWithResult` when authorization fails.\n12. `NotAuthorized` fallback can access `AuthorizationResult` by casting.\n13. Authorization succeeds when no authorization data applies.\n14. Existing validation for `ChildContent` and `Authorized` conflict remains unchanged.\n15. Existing validation for unsupported authentication schemes remains unchanged.\n\n### Recommended Test Names\n\n```csharp\nRendersForbiddenContentForAuthenticatedUnauthorizedUser\nRendersNotAuthorizedContentForAnonymousUnauthorizedUser\nFallsBackToNotAuthorizedWhenForbiddenIsNotSupplied\nForbiddenReceivesAuthorizationStateWithResult\nForbiddenCanAccessAuthorizationFailureReason\nForbiddenCanAccessMultipleAuthorizationFailureReasons\nNotAuthorizedFallbackReceivesAuthorizationStateWithResult\nNotAuthorizedFallbackCanAccessAuthorizationFailureReason\nRendersAuthorizedContentWhenAuthorizationSucceedsEvenWhenForbiddenIsSupplied\nRendersAuthorizedContentWhenAuthorizeDataIsNull\n```\n\n---\n\n### E2E Tests\n\nAdd E2E tests using a policy that fails with a custom authorization handler.\n\nScenario:\n\n1. Sign in as an authenticated user.\n2. User does not have required permission.\n3. Policy fails with:\n\n```text\nMissing permission: Project.Read\n```\n\nVerify:\n\n1. `Forbidden` content renders when supplied.\n2. Failure reason is shown in `Forbidden`.\n3. `NotAuthorized` fallback can show the failure reason when `Forbidden` is not supplied.\n4. Existing authentication layout still renders correctly.\n\n---\n\n## Documentation Updates\n\nDocumentation should cover:\n\n1. New `Forbidden` fragment.\n2. my case, I have custom localization service (like `IStringLocalizer`), that retrieve localization from database for user-specific culture. User culture configures in user settings, that may changes in application runtime, i.e. without page reload.\r\n\r\n```\r\nILocalizationService\r\n{\r\n\tstring this[string key] { get; }\r\n\tstring GetString(string key);\r\n\tvoid ChangeLanguage(CultureInfo culture);\r\n}\r\n```\r\n\r\nService registers as scoped, i.e. each user have own `ILocalizationService` with own specific culture settings.\r\n```\r\nservices.AddScoped\u003cILocalizationService, LocalizationService\u003e();\r\n```\r\nIn components this works great, just inject service.\r\n```\r\n@page \"/some-page\"\r\n@inject ILocalizationService T\r\n\u003ch1\u003e@T[\"SomeText\"]\u003c/h1\u003e\r\n```\r\n\r\nOf course, this does not work in standard case of using data annotation attributes. For example:\r\n\r\n```\r\nUser\r\n{\r\n\t[Required]\r\n\t[Display(Name = \"Name\")]\r\n\tstring Name { get; set; }\r\n\t\r\n\t[Display(Name = \"Email\")]\r\n\tstring Email { get; set; }\r\n}\r\n```\r\n\r\nData annotation attributes can be provided with custom type with localized strings. Something like this:\r\n\r\n```\r\nUser\r\n{\r\n\t[Required(ErrorMessageResourceName = \"Validation_Required\", ErrorMessageResourceType = typeof(LocalizationResources))]\r\n\t[Display(Name = \"Name\", ResourceType = typeof(LocalizationResources))]\r\n\tstring Name { get; set; }\r\n\t\r\n\t[Display(Name = \"Email\", ResourceType = typeof(LocalizationResources))]\r\n\tstring Email { get; set; }\r\n}\r\n\r\nLocalizationResources\r\n{\r\n\tpublic static string Name =\u003e GetString();\r\n\tpublic static string Email =\u003e GetString();\r\n\tpublic static string Validation_Required =\u003e GetString();\r\n\t\r\n\tpublic static Func\u003cILocalizationService\u003e LocalizationServiceProvider { get; set; }\r\n\r\n\tpublic static string GetString([CallerMemberName] string key = null)\r\n\t{\r\n\t\treturn LocalizationServiceProvider().GetString(key);\r\n\t}\r\n}\r\n```\r\n\r\nMain problem of this approach is that localized strings in `LocalizationResources` must be as static properties. So we cant directly inject user-specific `ILocalizationService`. But we can try get user-specific `ILocalizationService` via `Func\u003cILocalizationService\u003e LocalizationServiceProvider` that can be configured, for example, in `Configure()` method:\r\n\r\n```\r\npublic void Configure(IServiceProvider serviceProvider)\r\n{\r\n\tLocalizationResources.LocalizationServiceProvider = () =\u003e serviceProvider.GetRequiredService\u003cILocalizationService\u003e();\r\n}\r\n```\r\n\r\nOf course, this does not work, because of scope of `serviceProvider` in `Configure()` method differs from user-specific scopes. In order for this approach to work it is necessary in `LocalizationResources.LocalizationServiceProvider` uses some kind of context that will provide user-scoped `IServiceProvider` to resolve user-specific `ILocalizationService`.\r\n\r\nSo, at this moment, in server-side Blazor is exists any method to localize the data annotation attributes in non-resx scenarios? Have a plan to implement its in IMPORTANT: Comments are subject to validation constraints enforced by the MCP server - maximum 65536 characters for the complete comment (including footer which is added automatically), 10 mentions (@username), and 50 links. Exceeding these limits will result in an immediate error with specific guidance. NOTE: Discussion comments are disabled for this workflow because discussions:write permission is not available. INTENT ENCOURAGED: Include rationale (string, max 280 chars) and confidence (exactly one of: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH) with each call.
